models-fundamentals.summary: Know when concurrency helps, what each execution model costs, and how scaling laws and queueing limit the gains from adding threads, cores or nodes.
points: Concurrency is overlapping progress; parallelism is simultaneous execution. One core can be concurrent but never parallel.
Processes isolate memory and failures; threads share an address space and are cheaper; coroutines and goroutines switch in user space and cost a few KB each.
Amdahl's law: speedup = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/n), capped at 1 / (1 − p). Gustafson's law covers problems that grow with the machine.
The Universal Scalability Law adds contention (σ, a plateau) and coherency (κ, retrograde scaling) to explain why throughput can fall as nodes are added.
Little's law L = λW sizes concurrency: pools, connections and in-flight requests. For I/O-bound pools, threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute).
CPU-bound work wants about one worker per core; extra threads only add context switches and cache thrashing.
M:N schedulers (Go G-M-P, Java virtual threads, BEAM) multiplex many lightweight tasks onto few OS threads and hand off around blocking calls.
traps: Amdahl's law never predicts a slowdown; falling throughput comes from overheads such as coherency, switching or contention.
SMT siblings share one core, so 8 logical CPUs on 4 cores do not double CPU-bound throughput.
Cooperative schedulers (asyncio, pre-1.14 Go loops) stall every task when one task runs without yielding.
